pass_a_gloss: [...] to wall them, and to keep them outside every attack, and to show them better than the Babylonians. And in another way too they themselves were plundering together the nation of the Jews, on the one hand attacking them having been worn out, and seizing those left behind; on the other also dedicating to the falsely named gods sacred vessels, and sending out from the worship according to the Law, as from necessity, those who had come under the yokes of the slavery under them. And so God was saying through one of the holy prophets: And what also are you to me, Tyre and Sidon and all Galilee of foreigners? Are you paying back a repayment to me, or do you bear evil memory against me? Sharply and quickly I will pay back your repayment upon your heads, because you took my silver and my gold, and brought my choice and fine things into your temples, and the sons of Judah and the sons of Israel you gave away to the sons of the Greeks, so that you might push them out of their borders. So Tyre too was taken from the wrath of God, in some such way: for it was an island, a strait still having gone through the middle, and separating it from the mainland by not long distances. And when the Babylonian came and seeks to take it together with the others, he ordered the armies under hand to fill up the sea between, and to join it to the mainland, and to let it no longer remain an island. And this having happened, or being expected to be not long after, most of those in Tyre, inasmuch as having trade as their pursuit, and accustomed to sail by ships, swam off from the island with children and women together, and went away into other cities and villages. So the Babylonians, driving in, killed those who remained, and took many, and did the things customary to conquerors, but were grieved not moderately, having learned that very many, and of the very more prominent in it, putting their possessions in ships, had fled. And the account of the prophecy of Ezekiel also remembers the history. For thus the God of all said to him: Son of man, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon enslaved his force in a great slavery against Tyre. Every head baldness, and every shoulder stripped bare, and wages did not come to him and to his force, in return for the hard slavery which he slaved against Tyre. In return for this I have given him land of Egypt. For after the capture of the Tyrians the Babylonian was transferring the battle to the nation of the Egyptians. This history the blessed prophet Isaiah now remembers, and orders the ships of Carthage to wail. And to wail clearly [over] Tyre, because it perished, and they no longer come from land of the Kitians. They say [the section breaks off].
pass_b_english: … to wall them in, to keep them beyond the reach of any attack, and to show them stronger than the Babylonians.

In another way, too, they themselves joined in plundering the nation of the Jews: on the one hand by falling on them when they were worn down and seizing those who were left; on the other by dedicating sacred vessels to their falsely named gods, and by driving those who had come under the yoke of slavery to them away, by force as it were, from the worship the law prescribes. And so God said through one of the holy prophets: “And what are you to me, Tyre and Sidon and all Galilee of the foreigners? Are you paying me back, or do you bear a grudge against me? Swiftly and speedily I will return your payment on your own heads, because you took my silver and my gold, and carried my choice and fine things into your temples, and you sold the sons of Judah and the sons of Israel to the sons of the Greeks, to drive them out of their own borders” (Joel 3:4–6).

So Tyre too was captured through the wrath of God, in this way. It was an island, with a strait still running between, which separated it from the mainland by no great distance. When the Babylonian came and sought to take it along with the other cities, he ordered the armies under his command to fill in the sea between, to join it to the mainland, and to let it remain an island no longer. When this had been done, or was expected to be done before long, most of those in Tyre, since trade was their occupation and they were used to sailing, sailed away from the island with their children and wives and went off to other cities and villages.

The Babylonians then marched in, killed those who remained, took many captive, and did what victors usually do. Yet they were grieved not a little to learn that a great many, among them the most prominent in the city, had put their goods on ships and fled.

The prophecy of Ezekiel also records this history. For the God of all spoke to him thus: “Son of man, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made his army serve a great service against Tyre; every head was made bald, and every shoulder rubbed bare, yet neither he nor his army received any wages for the hard service he served against Tyre. In return for this I have given him the land of Egypt” (Ezekiel 29:18–20). For after the capture of the Tyrians the Babylonian turned the war against the nation of the Egyptians.

This is the history the blessed prophet Isaiah now recalls, when he commands the ships of Carthage to wail. They are to wail, clearly, over Tyre, because it has perished, and they no longer come from the land of the Kittim (Isaiah 23:1). They say …

choices.why: Tyre and its allies plundered the Jews; the Jews are not the plunderers.

choices.english: driving those who had come under the yoke
choices.why: They forced the captives away from the worship of the Law.
Joel 3:4 Septuagint: to remember wrongs against someone.
ἀπονήχομαι, literally 'swam off', is used here of escaping by ship.
The Septuagint renders Tarshish in Isaiah 23:1 as Carthage; Cyril follows it.
